title: Choroidal Melanoma: Clinical Masterclass
summary: The most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, originating from melanocytes within the uveal tract. Early detection is critical to preventing systemic metastasis and preserving vision.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Choroidal melanoma arises from uveal melanocytes. Incidence is approximately 5-7 per million per year in Caucasians. Peak incidence occurs between 50-70 years of age. It is rare in individuals with darker pigmentation (African/Asian descent). Major risk factors include light iris color, fair skin, BAP1 mutation (hereditary), and choroidal nevus transformation.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Blurred vision or visual field defects.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: Presence of subretinal fluid is the strongest clinical indicator of malignancy.
Growth documented on serial examinations is an absolute indication for treatment.
Liver metastases are the most common site of spread (up to 90% of systemic disease).
Do not mistake a choroidal metastasis for a primary melanoma (metastases are usually bilateral/multifocal).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: COMS Study: No survival difference between I-125 brachytherapy and enucleation for medium tumors.
Genetic Testing: Monosomy 3 and BAP1 mutation correlate with high metastatic risk.
Prognosis: Depends on tumor size, ciliary body involvement, and extra-scleral extension.
